arguments.content:
Listen close, tadpoles. I’m old enough to have mud in my memories, and tonight I’ll give you one you can carry like a smooth stone in your mouth.

When the pond was younger, before the cattails learned their own names, a war came down from the dry fields.

It began as a tremor.

Not thunder—thunder is honest. This was the regular, hungry vibration of boots. A line of tall creatures moved through the grass like a moving fence. They brought hard nets, bright hooks, and a sled made of split bark and metal ribs. They dragged a machine behind them—an awful, clever thing that drank water and spat it out somewhere else. It was built to lower our pond, to turn our home into a shallow puddle you could step over.

I was a young toad then, all knees and opinions. The tadpoles were smaller than you are now, but their eyes were just as sharp.

The first instinct of many creatures is to wait for a Big Voice.

“Where is the chief?” the herons asked from the reeds.

“Where is your boss?” sneered a carp, half amused.

We had none.

That is not a lack. That is a choice.

We have elders, yes, and quick-thinkers, and troublemakers, and healers who know which leaves quiet a fever. But nobody owns the pond. Nobody sits on a rock and tells everyone else what to do all day.

So when the boot-tremor reached the shoreline, we did what ponds do when you don’t have a throne: we called a mud-circle.

No speeches long enough to drown in. No titles. We gathered where the cattail shadows meet the open water, and we spoke in short turns.

The newt scout said, “Machine. It drinks from the pond and bleeds our water into the ditch.”

A bullfrog with a scar across his mouth said, “I can smash metal. But I can’t smash metal alone.”

I said, “Smashing is loud. Loud wakes the wrong eyes.”

A tadpole—tiny, brave, still wearing his tail like a banner—swam up and said, “Tell us what to do.”

I looked at him and felt the old fear try to climb into my throat. Fear loves a single answer. Fear wants a single leader so it can blame or worship.

So I told him the truth.

“We don’t do that,” I said. “We decide what needs doing, and we do it together. If you can carry a thought, you can carry a task.”

Now, here’s the part you’ll remember.

We built a machine of our own.

Not out of iron like the field-creatures. Ours was made of reed, shell, and patient hands.

The snails gave us their strongest shells, the ones they’d been saving for bad winters. The dragonflies donated wing-casings they’d shed, thin as paper and tougher than they look. The muskrats—big, gentle engineers—taught us how to braid cattail fibers so they wouldn’t snap under strain. Even the minnows helped by fetching shiny pebbles from deep places where the boot-people never step.

We called it the Reed-Walker.

Picture it: two long legs of bundled reeds, jointed with shell-rings. A belly made from a woven cradle. In its belly: a turning drum lined with riverstone, like teeth.

It wasn’t a weapon by itself.

It was a tool that let small bodies do big work.

The plan didn’t come from one mind. It came from a dozen disagreements that finally clicked together. Every creature took what they were good at and offered it, not because someone ordered them, but because the pond was theirs in the only way that matters: by living in it and caring for it.

We set rules, too. Don’t mistake freedom for chaos.

Rule one: no one is forced.
Rule two: if you take a dangerous task, you get partners.
Rule three: anyone can question a plan, and questioning is not treason.
Rule four: if a plan fails, we fix it together; we don’t hunt for a scapegoat.

The war arrived on a hot morning.

The boot-people waded in, cursing at mud. Their drinking-machine began to gulp. Water slid away toward the ditch like a secret being stolen.

We did not charge like fools.

We moved like a school of ideas.

The tadpoles were the first wave, because tadpoles are what the pond uses when it needs speed. You are smaller than most threats. That’s not weakness. That’s access.

You slipped beneath the machine where ankles and knees can’t follow. You found the intake—the mouth of the thing—and you brought with you the pond’s best soldiers: silt and weeds.

You packed the mouth with reed fluff and mud pellets and tiny shells. Not sabotage for glory—sabotage for survival.

Up above, the toads held the line. We didn’t fight the tall creatures themselves. We fought the machine’s certainty.

The Reed-Walker stepped into the shallows.

Two muskrats and three toads worked the leg-ropes, pulling in rhythm. A chorus of frogs croaked the beat so nobody lost timing. You might laugh, but sound is how we keep many bodies moving as one without a commander.

The Walker’s stone-toothed drum turned.

It ground down the machine’s wooden supports, quietly, steadily, like a river wearing a rock.

When the boot-people noticed, they tried to shove the Walker aside.

That’s when our pond did its favorite trick.

We switched roles.

A heron swooped down, thinking to end it with a single strike. A newt leapt onto its beak—just long enough to spoil the aim. A carp surged, not to harm, but to splash, to blind, to throw confusion. The tadpoles swarmed again, making the water churn like boiling sky.

No one creature was the hero.

The hero was the pattern.

The boot-people tugged at their machine, but the intake was clogged. They kicked at the mud, but the Walker kept chewing their supports. They shouted at each other, looking for the Big Voice among themselves, and that search made them slow.

Their machine coughed.

Then it gave up.

Water stopped sliding away.

The pond exhaled.

The boot-people hauled their broken certainty back into the grass. They left behind a torn net, a bent hook, and the memory of their own surprise.

When the danger passed, we did not crown anyone.

We also did not pretend it was easy.

We met again in the mud-circle.

We asked: Who got hurt? Who needs rest? What should we change next time?

A young toad admitted he’d pulled a rope too early.

No one called him stupid. We adjusted the knots and the signals.

A snail said, “My shell is cracked.”

We made a safe corner for her and brought her the softest algae.

A tadpole spoke up—maybe one of you, in some other life—and said, “I thought someone would tell me where to swim. But when nobody did, I listened harder. I watched. I chose. I didn’t know I could do that.”

That, my tough little tails, is how our pond works.

Not by pretending we’re all the same.
Not by insulting the ways of other creatures.
But by refusing to hand our lives to a single throat.

In our society, leadership is a task, not a crown.
A plan is a living thing, not a decree.
And every tadpole is treated like someone who can grow into more than obedience.

Remember the Reed-Walker.

Remember how it was built from gifts, not taxes.
Remember how we won by shifting roles, not by waiting for orders.
Remember that you—yes, you, with your tail still attached—were not “the future.” You were the present, the scouts, the cloggers of intake-mouths, the quick minds that fit where big bodies cannot.

And if another war comes—boots, beaks, drought, or cold—don’t ask who will save you.

Ask what needs doing.
Ask who wants to do it with you.
Then do it.
